newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Moslems among Rwandan refugees agree to go home.
newsitem.headline: Moslems among Rwandan refugees agree to go home.

text.p: The Moslems among the 540,000 Rwandan refugees in Tanzania have agreed to go home to Rwanda under a repatriation plan announced by Tanzania and the United Nations, a U.N. official said on Wednesday.
The Moslem refugees, who number between 10,000 and 13,000, want to go home by next weekend, said Musa Abiriga, head of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR.
"We have received a request from the Moslem community that we should facilitate their going back to Rwanda on Saturday," Abiriga told reporters in the west Tanzanian town of Ngara.

The Moslems are outside the Hutu/Tutsi divide in Rwandan society and few played any part in the massacres in Rwanda in 1994, when militant Hutus killed off up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
They are the largest single group to sign up for the repatriation plan since the UNHCR and the Tanzanian authorities said last week the refugees must go home by December 31.
The response to the plan has been muted and UNHCR officials said on Wednesday only 3,300 people had gone home so far.

Abiriga said that according to latest UNCHR figures the number of refugees who broke out of two northern camps on Sunday and Monday was about 16,000 and at least 2,500 of these had since turned up at another refugee camp at Chabalisa.
The UNHCR had earlier given different figures for the size of the breakout -- anywhere from 1,000 to 23,000 people.
Most of those who abandoned the camps are hiding in the Tanzanian bush, apparently to avoid repatriation.

Some of the refugees do not want to go home for fear of prosecution or revenge attacks by relatives of people killed in 1994. Aid workers say members of the Hutu militia the Interahamwe have also been telling them scare stories about the fate they will meet if they return to Rwanda.
The Tanzanian army has about 10,000 men in the region but it has not yet tried to round up the fugitives.
Abiriga said the Tanzanian government had told U.N. and other agencies that it would not use force to repatriate the refugees at least until the deadline expires on January 1.
But it will enforce a rule that refugees cannot stray more than four km (2.5 miles) from the camps.
"The position of the government is that any refugee who goes ...out of the four km zone will have broken the law," he said.
He said the UNHCR took courage from the gradual increase in the number of refugees registering to go home. Out of the 3,300 who have left, 1,928 left on Tuesday, he said.
"This is the beginning hopefully of a major repatriation from this end...We feel the figures are still low but we're optimistic. The figures are increasing day by day," he said.
